thread.title: Williamson County inks incentives agreement for $1B Apple campus

author: Daniel Salazar
title: Williamson County inks incentives agreement for $1B Apple campus
text: – Staff Writer, Austin Business Journal Dec 18, 2018, 12:08pm PST Texas once again opened the checkbook to win an economic development prize from California. In the latest foray from the Lone Star State, Williamson County leaders have approved incentives for the large campus that Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) plans to build in North Austin. County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to enter into a so-called Chapter 381 economic development agreement with the Cupertino-based technology company. Under the agreement, Apple agreed to spend at least $400 million purchasing and developing land in Robinson Ranch over 15 years. The facility's first phase will have a minimum assessed value of $50 million by the end of 2022. When Apple announced the new campus last week, it said it would invest $1 billion . To receive the Williamson County incentives, Apple needs to create 4,000 full-time equivalent jobs during the 15-year term of the agreement, which will begin the full tax year after the company's creation of the first 700 jobs. The employment goals in the incentives agreement steadily increase by increments of 600 jobs every two years for the agreement's first decade. A final increment of 300 additional jobs by the term's 12th anniversary would bring the total job count to 4,000. See also: Where Apple will employ the most people by 2022 In return, Williamson County will reimburse Apple 65 percent of its property taxes for 15 years. Chapter 381 refers to a section of state law that allows a local government like Williamson County to make public loans or grants to promote economic development and business activity. Apple, led by CEO Tim Cook , is also in line to get upwards of $25 million in payments from the state-run Texas Enterprise Fund, according to the Austin American-Statesman . Williamson County officials have touted how revenue from Apple's new campus will continue the area's boom times, particularly in boosted government services. "The tax that we'll see from that annually ... is breathtaking," Judge-Elect Bill Gravell told Austin Business Journal last week. "It's the best day Williamson County has had in many, many years because of the leadership of our current Williamson County Judge Dan Gattis and our current Commissioners Court." Austin Chamber of Commerce Board Chairman Phil Wilson said it took months of hard work from Williamson County and Apple "to get us here today." "The potential for up to 15,000 good paying jobs across all skill levels represents new opportunities for someone to get a job, advance their career, pay their bills and provide for their families," Wilson said in a statement. "Up to $1 billion of investment is a number that speaks for itself and is an influx of capital that will provide other jobs as the new campus begins construction." University of Texas professor Nate Jensen , who specializes in economic incentive deals, questions if the agreement was necessary to secure Apple's new investment. "It's not a question whether they're going to add value to Williamson County," he said. "The question is whether you had to give anything for them to come here." Jensen added that expansions of existing corporate locations are much less driven by incentives. "Most of the research suggests that expansion projects are much more likely to have occurred without incentives," he said. Last week, Apple also unveiled plans for new sites in Seattle, San Diego and Culver City, Calif. with expansions in Pittsburgh, New York and Boulder, Colo. Ranked by Local employee headcount Rank
